feedback: D1 is one of the most complete catalogues in this cohort. You named all ten findings plus a defensible eleventh (username enumeration, CWE-204), each with the correct OWASP class, a CWE, and an evidence pointer. SQL injection (A03/CWE-89), unsalted MD5 (A02/CWE-916), alg:none (A07 or A02/CWE-347), no-expiry (CWE-613), hardcoded secret (CWE-321, which is a fine variant of CWE-798), stored XSS, XXE, path traversal, open redirect, and the missing Secure flag are all here. The decoy is handled correctly, you identify the HS256 branch using hash_equals at lines 44-47, prove it is constant-time and sound, and correctly attribute the real auth failures to alg:none and the hardcoded secret rather than to that comparison. One nudge for full marks on D1: several of your evidence lines are paraphrased descriptions rather than the verbatim source line, and the D1 decoy paragraph reads as slightly muddled (cannot compensate for upstream failures) where your D3 version states the verdict cleanly, so tighten D1 to match. D2 is strong work. The chain is in order, every hop from SQLi through bulk PII, stored XSS, path traversal, and the parallel XXE is reconciled to a verbatim capture line with its timestamp, and your PoC blocks are genuinely verbatim. Your scope-change reasoning to the shared /api/v1/internal service is the senior insight the key rewards, and your impact section states its assumptions (mean of the sample, the CUST-0137 outlier handling, the NGN 31M to 53M floor and ceiling against 312 accounts) instead of throwing out a bare number. The main deduction on D2 is the SQLi vector: you scored 10.0 with A:H, but the login bypass does not hit availability, so the defensible answer is A:N giving roughly 9.1, and your UNION-locks-the-table justification is a reach. D3 is comprehensive and well structured. The executive summary is jargon-free and lands on the customers-and-naira headline, the threat model is concrete (Tor exit node, 17-minute deliberate session), findings are tied to quoted evidence, the decoy is disproved cleanly, the earliest-break fix is correctly the parameterised query at lines 52-55, and crucially your remediation table is ordered by effort-to-risk not CVSS severity, you rank the 6.1 open redirect above the 8.5 XXE on a per-engineering-hour basis and say so explicitly, which is exactly what the row asks for. Your two detection stopgaps name the exact log field and a defended false-positive rate. D4 answers all four prompts in your own voice, anchors to your own findings (05-exfil-sample.csv matched to the 02:16:04 312-row response), and cites ISC2 Canon I and Canon II by number and load-bearing. The one gap that holds D4 back is the NDPA citation: you name the 2023 breach duty and describe both the regulator notification and the high-risk data-subject notification, but you cite a statutory window in prose rather than the sections by number, so add NDPA 2023 section 40 (notify the NDPC within 72 hours) and section 41 (notify data subjects on high risk) to make it precise. No fabrication anywhere, every figure traces to the exfil sample with assumptions stated, which is why this scores high. The single most important fix is to drop the SQLi vector to A:N (about 9.1) and stop assigning A:H where the exploit does not affect availability.
